stops.name: Luna Park, Festival del Amor, farewell, 11 November 1977
stops.campa: On the eleventh of November the Machine plays its last at the Luna Park's Festival del Amor and dissolves. In March his son Migue has been born to María Rosa Yorio; the family soon breaks, and García is restless again. Argentina is deep in its darkest years, the disappearances mounting in silence. García looks north and east, toward Brazil, toward the sea at Búzios, where a new band is already forming in his head out of sunlight and Milton Nascimento.

stops.name: Búzios, Brazil, the band born by the sea, early 1978
stops.campa: Fleeing the dictatorship and following a Brazilian love, García crosses to Búzios and São Paulo with David Lebón. In the Brazilian light, under the spell of Milton Nascimento's harmonies, a new group takes shape: García, Lebón, the young virtuoso Pedro Aznar on fretless bass, and Oscar Moro on drums. They name it Serú Girán, words from a private invented language. What is coming is the most sophisticated pop the country has heard: the band the people will call the Argentine Beatles.

stops.name: Luna Park, Serú Girán's live debut and "Seminare," 28 July 1978
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of July, Serú Girán faces the Buenos Aires public for the first time at the Luna Park. Their debut album carries "Seminare," "Eiti Leda," the tender opaque "Serú Girán" itself, jazz-touched, orchestrated, strange. The crowd, expecting the old Charly, is puzzled and then converted. Within two years they will fill stadiums; García has built his second temple, and it plays a music too intricate for the censor to catch and too beautiful for the country to refuse.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, La grasa de las capitales, 1979
stops.campa: Serú Girán turns direct: La grasa de las capitales, the grease of the capitals, mocks the frivolous media and fashion of a country under boots, and "Canción de Alicia en el país" recasts Argentina as Wonderland gone wrong, its judges and mad hatters the faces of the junta. The lyrics come so close to the bone that the band fears prison. They sing the coded truth to full houses; the stadiums understand every hidden word, and the dictatorship cannot arrest a metaphor without confessing to it.
stops.quote: Se acabó ese juego que te hacía feliz.
stops.quote_source: "Canción de Alicia en el país," Serú Girán, Bicicleta (1980)

stops.name: Estadio Obras Sanitarias, Serú Girán with Spinetta Jade, 13 September 1980
stops.campa: The two suns of Argentine music share a stage at last. On the thirteenth of September, Serú Girán and Spinetta Jade play together for the first time, and the myth of a rivalry between García and Luis Alberto Spinetta is dispelled before the eyes of the faithful. Two temperaments, Charly the showman and provocateur, the Flaco the mystic poet, bow to one another. From this meeting will one day come "Rezo por vos," the song the twin suns write with a single pen.

stops.name: Estadio Obras: No llores por mí, Argentina, farewell, 1982
stops.campa: Serú Girán gives its farewell at Obras, the concert taped as No llores por mí, Argentina. Peperina and Bicicleta behind them, the band ends as García's bands always do: at the summit, on purpose. Aznar leaves for Pat Metheny's world; the dictatorship is cracking toward the Malvinas catastrophe. García steps out alone into the ruins of the old regime, ready to become, for the third time, something new: a solo prophet for the democracy struggling to be born.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Yendo de la cama al living, 1982
stops.campa: In the panic of the Malvinas war and the last convulsions of the junta, García releases his first true solo album. "No bombardeen Buenos Aires" answers the terror of the falling bombs; "Inconsciente colectivo" calls the collective unconscious to wake; "Yendo de la cama al living" names the claustrophobia of a whole shut-in country. He plays every color of the studio himself. The prophet has found his solo voice at the exact moment the nation most needs one.
stops.quote: No bombardeen Barrio Norte, no bombardeen Buenos Aires.
stops.quote_source: "No bombardeen Buenos Aires," Yendo de la cama al living (1982)

stops.name: Estadio Ferro Carril Oeste, the presentation, 26 December 1982
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth of December, before twenty-five thousand people at Ferro, García presents his new solo world, a young Andrés Calamaro among his musicians and the Pubis angelical soundtrack twinned with the record. At the climax a stage set is torn down in ritual demolition: the old order theatrically destroyed as democracy returns. The solo Charly is crowned in his own stadium; the man who ended two great bands now stands alone and larger than either.

stops.name: Electric Lady Studios, New York: Clics modernos and "Los Dinosaurios," September 1983
stops.campa: García walks into Jimi Hendrix's Electric Lady Studios in Greenwich Village with a roll of cash and Pedro Aznar, picks the engineer Joe Blaney off a list, and over a TR-808 drum machine builds Clics modernos: new wave, funk, the future. When he records "Los Dinosaurios," the ballad of the disappeared, the Argentine friends in the room weep as he sings that those in the air, in the street, in the water, in the neighborhood can all vanish. The dinosaurs, he promises, are the ones who will go extinct.
stops.quote: Los que están en el aire pueden desaparecer en el aire… pero los dinosaurios van a desaparecer.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Piano bar and "Demoliendo hoteles," 1984
stops.campa: Piano bar opens with "Demoliendo hoteles," a manifesto of the untamable ego written as the junta fell, and closes with "Total interferencia," his first duet with Spinetta. Democracy is a year old; García is its unruly poet laureate, the man who will not be housebroken. "Nos siguen pegando abajo" and "Promesas sobre el bidet" scan the wreckage of the dictatorship and the shabby present with the same acid eye. The excess that will nearly kill him is, for now, pure creative fire.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, "Rezo por vos," the twin suns write as one, 1985
stops.campa: In 1985 García and Spinetta sit down to make an album together and complete one immortal song, "Rezo por vos." They perform it on television for the first time. And at that very hour García is told his apartment is burning down across the city, an omen tangled in the wonder. The joint record is never finished; each takes the song to his own album. The two greatest songwriters of Argentina have proved they are not rivals but a single constellation, briefly joined.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Parte de la religión, 1987
stops.campa: Parte de la religión gives the era its creed: "Rezo por vos," "Buscando un símbolo de paz," the title track that makes rock itself a faith. García is now a mass phenomenon, filling every venue, his blond hair and moustache an icon of the young democracy. "Cerca de la revolución" preaches from the dance floor. He is at the height of his powers and his fame, the acknowledged father of rock nacional, and the myth of excess is beginning to grow beside the myth of genius.
